news.title: UEFA warns FIFA of legal action over failed World Cup sell-off plan
news.lede: European football body UEFA has threatened FIFA with legal action over Gianni Infantino’s failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to private investors, and said any potential evidence should not be destroyed. Infantino’s secretive proposal to raise US$4.2 billion (NZ$7.1 billion) from investors including the New York investment firm of Joshua Kushner was dropped Saturday, days after the revelation in media reports provoked a global furore. UEFA led the backlash, and on Friday its 55 member federations met to agree to boycott all FIFA events and competitions while the proposal was active. Now lawyers for UEFA have informed FIFA that the European body is “actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints ... arising out of and in connection with the FFE (FIFA Forward Enterprise) plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters”.

news.title: Atlanta ‘96 gold felt like World Cup — Lawal
news.lede: Garba Lawal, a member of Nigeria’s historic 1996 Olympic gold medal-winning football team, has told PUNCH Sports Extra that the Dream Team’s triumph in Atlanta remains the closest feeling to winning the World Cup, describing the achievement as the pinnacle of his football career. The 52-year-old insisted that the achievement cannot be compared with anything else Nigerian football has produced. Nigeria fielded a golden generation of players between 1994 and 1998 who could compete with any team in the world, reaching the World Cup on both occasions but falling short at the knockout stage each time. In between those campaigns, however, the Olympic Eagles won football gold at the 1996 Atlanta Games, a feat Lawal rates above what a World Cup run could have delivered.

news.title: Korea's football reckoning may yet turn World Cup disaster into reform
news.lede: Former national football team head coach Hong Myung-bo, right, answers lawmakers' questions while former Korea Football Association (KFA) President Chung Mong-gyu listens during a parliamentary hearing on alleged irregularities involving the KFA at the National Assembly in Seoul, Thursday. Yonhap Hong Myung-bo’s second spell in charge of Korea’s national team started amid jeers and boos at Seoul World Cup Stadium in September 2024. It ended with his resignation in late June and what followed was a reckoning just a few kilometers down the Han River at the National Assembly building in Yeouido. As a head coach, you know something has gone wrong on the football field when you end up in parliament.

news.title: "FIFA President's Grip Tightens, Dictatorship Unbearable... Resign Immediately" Football Scandal 'Turns the World Upside Down'
news.lede: Pressure for the resignation of FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who is facing fierce backlash over plans to sell stakes in the World Cup, has reached its peak. Opposition forces centered on the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) have drawn a line in the sand, warning that they will boycott if In Pan-ti-no (Chairman) does not step down. The British media outlet 'BBC' reported on the 4th (Korea time), "According to senior officials at UEFA, opponents of In Pan-ti-no (Chairman) are prepared to refuse cooperation with FIFA if he does not resign," and added, "Some opposition factions, facing severe repercussions from the withdrawal of the stake sale proposal, have vowed to fight to the end, stating they have nowhere left to retreat as long as In Pan-ti-no (Chairman) remains in office."

news.lede: US president Donald Trump will allegedly do “everything possible” to help Gianni Infantino remain as FIFA president as massive pressure comes from European governing body UEFA. Infantino’s presidency is under threat after his failed scheme to sell off 20 to 30 per cent of a new subsidiary to private investors. news.title: FIFA scrap World Cup sell-off plan after backlash
news.lede: This content is provided by Exco Player and may use cookies or similar technologies. Please click 'Allow and Continue' below to load the content. FIFA “will not proceed” with plans to sell stakes in a company which would run the commercial and operational aspects of its competitions, a statement from president Gianni Infantino said. The plan, which would include the men’s and women’s World Cups, has been rejected by three continental confederations with UEFA insisting its nations would boycott FIFA events.
